name: lockable-object
intent: Let an object own the lock that guards its state and publish that lock, so collaborators can satisfy multi-call invariants and condition waits explicitly instead of relying on synchronisation hidden inside individual methods.
problem: Collaborators must keep a shared object stable across a sequence of calls - read, decide and write; transfer between two objects; wait until a predicate holds - but the object's synchronisation is private and per-method, so no client can make the sequence atomic, wait on the same lock, or substitute a different locking policy.
context: Several threads or tasks share mutable objects inside one process and the unit of exclusion is the object (or a small set of objects): clients need compound atomic operations, condition waits on the same lock, pluggable locking policies, or visibility into contention.
benefits: Atomicity across calls: a collaborator can hold the lock while reading, deciding and updating, which a self-synchronising per-method API cannot express.
The synchronisation contract is explicit and reviewable: what guards the state, and in which order several objects are locked, is visible in the interface instead of hidden inside each method.

Locking policy becomes pluggable: the same object works with a mutex, a recursive lock, a read-write lock or a no-op lock for single-threaded builds (strategized locking), and can offer timed or try-lock acquisition.

Condition waits run on the right lock: waiting and signalling (guarded suspension, monitor-style wait/notify) require the caller to hold the lock that guards the predicate, which only a published lock allows.
Contention becomes observable: queueing, hold times and ownership can be measured at the lock object rather than inferred from latency.
Single-threaded and concurrent configurations can share one code path when the published lock is a no-op implementation.
tradeoffs: The object cannot enforce its own discipline: a collaborator that forgets the lock - or reaches the state through a back door - corrupts it silently; that is the price of moving exclusion to the client.
Deadlock risk moves from the library to the client: several published locks invite lock-order inversions that no single object can detect.

The lock becomes public interface: changing the internal concurrency strategy (splitting the state, switching to immutable snapshots or lock-free structures) is now a breaking change for every collaborator.
Hold time is controlled by the caller: I/O, callbacks or foreign code under the lock can stall every other user of the object indefinitely.

One lock per object serialises all of its operations, including independent ones (coarse-grained exclusion caps scalability), and the acquire/release pairs cost more than an inlined monitor in the uncontended case.
Hand-written acquire/release pairs leak the lock on early returns and exceptions unless every call site goes through a scoped guard.

participants.responsibility: Owns the shared state and the lock that guards it; keeps the state private and publishes the lock - a lock-typed member, an accessor, or a lock interface - as part of its contract.
The mutual-exclusion primitive a collaborator must hold: mutex, recursive lock, read-write lock, spin lock or no-op lock; it defines the exclusion domain of the object's state.
Acquires the published lock around every access or compound operation, through the language's scoped guard where one exists, and follows the documented acquisition order.
Chooses which lock implementation is published and how it is acquired (blocking, timed, try, fair), keeping concurrency policy out of the object's application logic.

use_cases: Registries and caches with get-or-create semantics: the caller reads, decides and inserts under one lock instead of racing between separate synchronised calls.
Transfers between two objects: both publish their lock, so the client acquires them in one documented global order and updates both atomically.
Deployments where the same class needs different synchronisation: mutex under contention, read-write lock for read-mostly state, no-op lock in single-threaded builds (strategized locking).
Predicate-driven workers: a consumer holds the object's published lock, waits on its condition and re-checks the predicate before proceeding (guarded suspension).
Contention-aware front doors: the lock object exposes queue length and hold time for metrics, and try-lock acquisition implements admission control under overload.
Deterministic concurrency tests: a test acquires the published lock to hold a worker at a chosen point and asserts the invariant that must hold there.

Connection-pool management: a pool publishes its lock so callers can acquire and release connections atomically within a transaction, avoiding connection-leak races and get-or-create thundering-herds.

Entity-component systems with shared mutable state: components that cross system boundaries are guarded by their owner's published lock so systems can read, validate and update a component atomically without holding the entire world lock.

Read-mostly caches with periodic invalidation: a read-write lock variant lets readers proceed concurrently while a single writer holds exclusive access during cache refresh; the lockable object's published lock is the read-write lock itself.

Deterministic simulation and testing: a simulated process or game loop uses a lockable object's published lock to pause a worker at an injection point (yield) and assert invariants, then resumes — the same pattern used in time-travel debuggers.

Java resource owners can publish a dedicated java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock to trusted collaborators; reentrancy, timed tryLock, newCondition and queue/hold diagnostics support compound operations and guarded waits while callers still bracket unlock in finally.

Portable in-process resource adapters can use Python's threading.Condition with an existing Lock or RLock, while .NET's System.Threading.Lock provides the analogous dedicated lock member with scoped EnterScope and timed TryEnter acquisition.

Rust's std::sync::Mutex<T> binds protected data to its lock and exposes access through MutexGuard RAII; sharing an Arc<Mutex<T>> gives collaborators shared ownership without separating the state from its exclusion guard.
avoid_when: No caller ever needs a multi-call atomic section or a condition wait: keep the lock private behind synchronised methods (monitor object) or make the value immutable.
The object can be confined to one thread, task or actor: ownership or isolation removes the need for any lock.
The object is a value that gets copied or serialised: a copied lock duplicates the discipline and splits one critical section into two.
Contention itself is the bottleneck: lock-free structures, queues or striping beat publishing a single coarser lock.
The state can live in a message-passing owner (channel, actor, worker): communicate instead of sharing.
anti_patterns: Publishing the object's own monitor as the lock (synchronized(this), lock(this), locking on a Type object or an interned string): foreign code and subclasses can take the same lock and deadlock unrelated components.
Acquire/release pairs written by hand instead of a scoped guard: one early return and the lock stays held.
Holding the published lock during I/O, callbacks or foreign calls: hold time becomes unbounded and lock inversion likely.
Ad-hoc ordering when several lockable objects are locked (A-then-B in one path, B-then-A in another) - the classic deadlock the pattern makes possible.
"Lockable" as decoration: the lock is published but the state is also reachable through an unlocked back door, so the invariant is not actually protected.
design_principles: Encapsulation with an explicit seam: publish the locking interface, never the state; the published lock is the only synchronisation surface.
Separation of concerns: concurrency policy (which lock, acquired how) stays independent of the object's application logic (strategized locking).
Explicit contracts over implicit behaviour: what the lock protects and the order in which locks are taken belong to the type's documented contract.
Scope-bound resource management: every acquisition is paired with a lexical scope (RAII, try/finally, with), so all exit paths release.
Least exposure: hand the lock only to collaborators that need it; callers without compound-atomicity needs are better served by synchronised methods.
best_practices: Use timed lock acquisition (tryLock with timeout) in any code path that might be called by a different thread holding another lock — it prevents indefinite blocking and is the basis of deadlock-detection test harnesses.

Prefer lock striping (a fixed-size array of independent locks) over a single coarse lock when the state is partitionable and contention is high; this limits the critical section to the partition rather than the whole structure.

Be copy-aware in value-semantics languages: a mutex (Go sync.Mutex, C++ std::mutex) copied after construction is a distinct, unlocked mutex — the original lock is unrelated to the copy. Pass by pointer or embed the mutex as a struct field, never copy the container.

In languages with async/await, avoid awaiting while holding a lock — async lock acquisition can yield the task, letting another task acquire the same lock and deadlock. Use blocking mutexes for the critical section, not async mutexes, unless the critical section is provably short and non-reentrant.

Expose lock diagnostics (queue length, hold time, ownership) through a monitoring interface rather than ad-hoc logging; this decouples observation from production logic and keeps the published interface narrow.
When substituting a read-write lock, validate that readers never mutate state; a writer that calls a read-only method under the same lock as a writer creates a priority-inversion or convoy issue.
Give the object a dedicated lock object (or lock-typed field, e.g. System.Threading.Lock) instead of using the object's own monitor, and expose it through a narrow accessor.

Acquire through the language's scoped idiom (lock_guard/scoped_lock, lock/withLock/synchronized, with lock:, mutex.synchronize, Mutex.withLock) and never write a bare acquire without a matching release on every path.

Define and document a global lock order; when two locks must be held, use the runtime's deadlock-avoiding multi-lock helper (std::scoped_lock/std::lock) or a fixed ordering, and prefer try-lock with timeout where liveness matters.
Keep critical sections short: compute and perform I/O outside the lock, update invariants inside it, and never call foreign code while holding it.
Make the lock policy configurable (mutex, read-write, recursive, no-op) and test the single-threaded and contended configurations of the same class.
Pair the published lock with the diagnostics the design needs (hold time, queue length, ownership) instead of bolting on a debug lock later.
sources: Williams, Anthony. 'C++ Concurrency in Action: Practical Multithreading' (Manning, 2019, 2nd ed.) — Chapters 3 and 4 cover std::mutex, std::lock, lock ordering for deadlock avoidance, and std::scoped_lock, which directly govern how a published lock is acquired and combined with other locks. https://www.manning.com/books/c-plus-plus-concurrency-in-action-second-edition

Oracle Java Documentation — 'Explicit Monitor Locks' section of the Java Tutorials covers the Lock interface, ReentrantLock, and the contrast with intrinsic synchronization (synchronized keyword), including the tryLock() non-blocking acquisition pattern and fairness policies. https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/essential/concurrency/locksync.html

Rustonomicon (The Rust Unstable Book) — 'Futures and the Mutex' section documents the Send+Sync bounds required for a Mutex<T> to be shared across task boundaries, plus the interaction between parking_lot::Mutex and async code. https://doc.rust-lang.org/nomicon/

Go Language Specification — The Locker interface (sync.Locker) and value-copy semantics for struct-based mutexes; also the Go Blog 'Go Concurrency Patterns' covers mutex usage in the context of goroutines and channels. https://go.dev/ref/spec

Java Design Patterns catalog (java-design-patterns.com), 'Lockable Object' - also known as Resource Lock and Mutual Exclusion Object; its Java example has the object implement a Lockable acquire/release interface instead of relying on the synchronized keyword alone.

Schmidt, Stal, Rohnert & Buschmann, Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 2: Patterns for Concurrent and Networked Objects (2000) - the synchronization patterns (Scoped Locking, Strategized Locking, Thread-Safe Interface) that govern how a published lock is acquired and parameterised; POSA2 does not itself name Lockable Object.

Goetz, Peierls, Bloch, Bowbeer, Holmes & Lea, Java Concurrency in Practice (2006) - intrinsic locks versus explicit Lock objects, lock ordering and hold-time discipline (cited by the Lockable Object entry above).

Java Design Patterns — 'Lockable Object Pattern in Java' defines the Resource Lock and Mutual Exclusion Object aliases and describes object-managed acquisition for shared resources. https://java-design-patterns.com/patterns/lockable-object/

Oracle Java SE 23 API — ReentrantLock provides reentrancy, fairness, timed tryLock, lock-associated conditions, queue/hold inspection, and the recommended try/finally release discipline. https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/23/docs/api/java.base/java/util/concurrent/locks/ReentrantLock.html

Python 3 threading documentation — Condition can use a supplied Lock or RLock, releases and reacquires it around wait, and supports context-manager scoping. https://docs.python.org/3/library/threading.html

Microsoft Learn — System.Threading.Lock documents EnterScope/using, TryEnter timeouts, exception-safe release, consistent multi-lock ordering, and the prohibition on await between enter and exit. https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.threading.lock?view=net-10.0

Rust standard library documentation — std::sync::Mutex<T> binds protected data to the mutex and exposes it through RAII guards, including Arc<Mutex<T>> sharing examples. https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/sync/struct.Mutex.html

SEI CERT LCK00-J — warns that exposing an intrinsic/public monitor to untrusted code enables denial-of-service contention and deadlock, and recommends private lock objects in that boundary case. https://wiki.sei.cmu.edu/confluence/x/djdGBQ
